C1.statement: There should be one, and preferably only one, obvious way to do something, so that code converges on shared idioms rather than diverging into clever variants.

C2.statement: Readability counts: code is read far more often than it is written, so the language should make the reader's job easy even at the writer's expense.

C3.statement: Explicit is better than implicit, and simple is better than complex, so behavior should be stated plainly rather than hidden in magic.

C4.statement: Executable pseudocode: the language should be clean and uncluttered enough that well-written code looks like the description of the algorithm itself.

C5.statement: Batteries included: a broad standard library ships with the language so common tasks need no external machinery.

C6.statement: We are all consenting adults: the language favors convention and trust over enforced access restrictions, leaving the programmer responsible rather than locked out.

C7.statement: Practicality beats purity: real-world usefulness takes precedence over theoretical consistency, and special cases are tolerated when they genuinely help.
